## Research question

The [PhD proposal's RQ1](../../phd/index.qmd) asks *which statistical, econometric and ML
methods most reliably identify market states out of sample*. Reliability, though, is not
self-defining. A method can produce a stable, plausible, well-recovered state estimate that
makes no difference to any decision. So this experiment tests the question underneath:

> **Does conditioning on a market-state estimate improve out-of-sample forecast calibration
> or risk control, *beyond what a continuous volatility signal using the same information
> already provides*?**

That final clause is the entire design. Comparing a state-conditional model against
buy-and-hold, or against nothing, would only demonstrate that volatility is informative —
which nobody disputes. The benchmark here is a model that sees the **same volatility
features and simply does not see the state**. Whatever the state adds over that, and only
that, is the incremental value of state information.

## Hypothesis

From the proposal's own position, and from what this lab has already found in
[regime-conditioning](../regime-conditioning-oos/index.qmd) and
[regime-conditional calibration](../regime-conditional-calibration/index.qmd):

- **H-a.** State information will **not** improve direction forecasts. Expected null.
- **H-b.** State information **will** improve *volatility-regime* calibration.
- **H-c.** A state overlay on volatility targeting will **not** improve risk-adjusted
  outcomes beyond the volatility scaler itself.

H-a and H-c are predictions of failure. Stating them in advance is what makes the result
informative either way.

## Data & method

Daily Nasdaq-100, 2 January 2015 – 6 July 2026 (2,892 days). The scored sample is **not uniform
across methods**: the three baselines and BOCPD fit nothing and score 2,355 days, while the four
methods that estimate parameters — Kalman, HMM, Markov-switching and CUSUM — surrender a training
window and score 1,755. Each is therefore compared against a benchmark run over *its own* sample,
never against a benchmark that saw a different period. Eight state estimators — three transparent baselines (moving-average crossover,
trailing-return sign, EWMA slope), a Kalman local-linear-trend filter, a Gaussian HMM, a
Markov-switching regression, and CUSUM and BOCPD change-point detectors — all producing a
**filtered** probability vector over {down, range, up}. The harness's ninth estimator, a
do-nothing constant, is excluded here: a state that never changes carries no information to
test, so scoring it would only pad the comparison count and loosen the deflated bar. Every estimate is
causal: the value at time *t* uses only data up to *t*, enforced by an automated look-ahead
test rather than by inspection.

**Calibration.** Walk-forward logistic regression, purged by the label horizon, comparing
`[rv20, rv60]` against `[rv20, rv60, p_down, p_range, p_up]` on three five-day-ahead targets:
*direction* (return positive), *loss* (return below minus one trailing standard deviation),
and *volatility* (realised volatility above its trailing median). Scored by Brier; a negative
delta means the state helped.

**Significance.** Diebold-Mariano tests on the per-observation loss differential with
Newey-West standard errors, because overlapping five-day labels make the differentials
serially correlated and an i.i.d. error would manufacture significance. With 24 comparisons
the relevant bar is not 1.96: under the null the largest of *N* t-statistics is around
$\sqrt{2\ln N}$, so the [deflated](../backtest-overfitting/index.qmd) threshold is
**|t| > 2.52**. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR is reported alongside.

**Risk control.** Volatility targeting at 10% annualised, with and without a state overlay
that multiplies exposure by $(1 - p_{\text{down}})$ — pre-committed, and purely defensive so
that it can only ever *reduce* exposure. Net of 2bp costs on turnover.

## Results

**Direction: a unanimous null, and worse than null.** All eight estimators made direction
forecasts *worse* than the volatility-only benchmark (Brier deltas +0.0012 to +0.0092 on a
baseline of 0.2497). Two of those harms are significant past the deflated bar — `bocpd`
(t = +3.31) and `return_sign` (t = +3.20). On the *loss* target the pattern repeats, with
`bocpd` at t = +4.57 and `return_sign` at t = +3.84. **Four of the twenty-four comparisons are
significant harms; none of them is a benefit.**

**Volatility regime: two survivors, one convincing.** Only `ewma_slope` (−0.0171, t = −3.98,
FDR p = 0.0008) and `bocpd` (−0.0074, t = −2.60, FDR p = 0.038) clear the deflated bar. The
`ewma_slope` result is a ~7% relative improvement on a 0.2407 baseline and is the only one
comfortably clear of it.

**Risk control: the null holds, and the naive reading is a trap.** Each overlay is compared against
a volatility-target baseline run on its own sample — Sharpe 0.863 at 11.3% volatility for the
2,355-day methods, 0.852 at 11.2% for the 1,755-day ones, both with a −16.7% maximum drawdown:

| measure | how many of the 8 overlays improve on the baseline |
|---|---|
| raw maximum drawdown | **8 of 8** |
| Sharpe ratio | 1 of 8 |
| drawdown per unit of volatility | 3 of 8 |

Read raw drawdown alone and every single overlay "works". That is an artefact: the overlay can
only cut exposure, so it always ends up holding less, and a rule that holds less always shows a
shallower drawdown. Read risk-adjusted and the effect disappears. The one overlay with a higher
Sharpe (`ms_regression`, 0.913) pays for it with 11.6× annual turnover against the baseline's
7.0×.

## The verdict — and what it means for the proposal

**H-a confirmed, more strongly than predicted.** State does not merely fail to time returns;
for two methods it significantly degrades direction and loss forecasts relative to volatility
alone. Adding state where it does not belong is not free.

**H-b partly confirmed, and narrower than hoped.** One estimator shows a robust
volatility-calibration gain that survives multiple-testing correction. Seven do not.

**H-c confirmed.** The state overlay adds no risk-adjusted value beyond the volatility scaler.
The same de-risking is available for nothing by simply lowering the volatility target — no
model, no turnover.

This tightens the proposal's central position. "Market-state information is a calibration and
risk-control signal, not a return-timing signal" survives, but with two amendments: the
calibration benefit is **specific and rare** rather than general, and the risk-control half of
the claim does **not** hold once exposure is properly controlled for.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The awkward result.** The one estimator whose benefit survives correction is `ewma_slope` —
a simple exponentially-weighted trend rule that ranks *worst* on persistence, changing state
every ~5 days. It is a poor state estimator by every stability measure in the harness and the
best one by this decision-value measure. Any account of RQ1 has to explain that rather than
average it away.
:::

I tested the obvious explanation — that a rapidly oscillating state is just re-encoding
volatility through its own instability — by adding the estimator's own causal rolling flip
rate to the **baseline**, so the benchmark already sees the churn. The gain did not collapse;
it strengthened slightly (−0.0157 → −0.0171, t = −3.69 → −3.98). The confound is ruled out and
the mechanism remains unexplained, which is the honest place to leave it.

## Limitations

- **Single asset.** These twenty-four comparisons are Nasdaq-100 only. On a seven-asset panel
  the `ewma_slope` volatility gain replicated (mean −0.0138) while `bocpd` decayed with each
  widening of the sample (−0.0074 → −0.0047 → −0.0020) — the signature of a partly
  sample-specific result. The full-panel deflation, where the bar rises to |t| > 3.24 for 189
  comparisons, is the outstanding test.
- **Unequal samples across methods.** Each estimator is scored fairly against *its own* benchmark,
  so no single comparison is biased — but the fitted methods see 600 fewer days than the baselines,
  which include the 2015–2017 stretch. Ranking a fitted method against a baseline is therefore not
  quite like-for-like, and the survivor, `ewma_slope`, happens to be on the longer sample. A
  common-window re-run is the clean version of this test.
- **The DM test is slightly liberal.** Its empirical size measured ~0.07 against a nominal
  0.05, so borderline results deserve more scepticism than their p-values suggest.
- **One overlay rule.** $(1 - p_{\text{down}})$ is defensible and pre-committed but arbitrary;
  a different mapping from state to exposure could behave differently.
- **Index, not total return, and no borrowing constraint** on the leveraged volatility target.

## What I learned

The most useful thing this experiment produced was not a finding but a **discipline about
measurement**. Raw drawdown made every overlay look successful, and the correct comparison
reversed it. I have made that mistake in reverse before — reading a single seed as a result —
and the fix is the same both times: fix the comparison before reading the number.

The second lesson is how much a fair benchmark costs a hypothesis. Against buy-and-hold,
almost everything here would have looked like a win. Against a volatility-only model with the
same information, twenty-two of twenty-four comparisons are neutral or harmful. That is the
difference between a result and an artefact, and it is the standard the
[LLM-trading literature](../../phd/literature/li-2025-finsaber-llm-evaluation/index.qmd)
conspicuously fails to meet.
